narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 58.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile (1 out of 10), while students who were accepted averaged around the middle of their class (5.8). This low ranking signaled to the model a higher risk that you would struggle with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor, and it worked in your favor. At 38, your score sits slightly above the average of accepted students (37.2), which helped pull the prediction back toward passing. Unfortunately, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the impact of your class standing.

Your first-year class ranking came in third. Placing in the third decile (well below the accepted-student average of 6) added further weight toward predicting failure, though its influence was smaller than the other two factors.

Taken together, the model saw your consistently lower class rankings as the dominant signal, outweighing your solid LSAT performance. To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic record in any remaining coursework, consider retaking the LSAT if possible, and explore bar-preparation programs that target students with similar profiles. These steps can demonstrate growth and potentially change future predictions. (248 words)
